mainEntity.name: How accurate is this calorie estimate?

acceptedAnswer.text: It's a well-validated estimate for most people, but individual metabolism varies. Use it as a starting point and adjust based on your actual weight trend over a few weeks.

mainEntity.name: Why does activity level matter so much?

acceptedAnswer.text: Activity level scales your baseline metabolic rate to reflect real daily energy use — the difference between sedentary and very active can be 500+ calories a day.

mainEntity.name: Why am I not losing weight at my calculated deficit?

acceptedAnswer.text: Common causes include underestimating portion sizes, overestimating exercise calories burned, or a maintenance calorie level that's actually different from the formula's estimate — tracking actual results over a few weeks helps calibrate.

mainEntity.name: Is it safe to eat below my calculated deficit?

acceptedAnswer.text: Very low-calorie diets can risk nutrient deficiencies and muscle loss — most guidance suggests not going below roughly 1,200 calories/day for women or 1,500 for men without medical supervision.

mainEntity.name: Should I recalculate my calorie needs as I lose weight?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes — as body weight changes, so does your BMR and total calorie needs, so recalculating every few weeks during an active weight loss or gain phase keeps your target accurate.

mainEntity.name: Is a 500-calorie deficit always the right target?

acceptedAnswer.text: It's a common starting point for roughly 0.5kg/week of loss, but very large deficits can be hard to sustain and may risk muscle loss — a moderate, sustainable deficit is generally more effective long-term.

mainEntity.name: Why does my projected weight loss slow down over time?

acceptedAnswer.text: Because a lighter body burns fewer calories. If you keep eating the same amount, the gap between what you eat and what you burn narrows each week, so the rate of loss falls. The projection recalculates your maintenance calories weekly to reflect this.
